New places (all from places-canon): bethany, bethphage, olives, upperroom, gethsemane, caiaphas. jericho and temple are reused from data.js.

akeldama.name: Akeldama (Field of Blood)
akeldama.note: A potter's field bought with Judas' silver as a burial place for strangers. Since at least the 4th century it has been shown on the southern slope of the Hinnom Valley, where the Greek Orthodox Monastery of St Onuphrius stands among rock-cut tombs. Potters worked with the clay of this valley (Jeremiah 18–19).

bethany.name: Bethany
bethany.note: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about 2 miles (15 stadia, John 11:18) from Jerusalem, home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus. Today it is al-Eizariya, a name that comes from Lazarus. A rock-cut tomb honored as Lazarus's since at least the 4th century lies in the village.

bethphage.name: Bethphage
bethphage.note: A village near the top of the Mount of Olives, on the road from Bethany to Jerusalem. The name probably means "house of unripe figs." A Franciscan chapel at et-Tur, built in 1883, marks the traditional place where the disciples fetched the colt; the Palm Sunday procession starts there every year.

caiaphas.name: House of Caiaphas
caiaphas.note: The high priest's palace stood in the wealthy Upper City. Two traditions compete: the Armenian site on Mount Zion near the Cenacle, and the Church of St Peter in Gallicantu on the eastern slope of Zion, built in 1931 over rock-cut cellars.

gethsemane.name: Gethsemane
gethsemane.note: An olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from the Temple. The name means "oil press." The Church of All Nations (1924), built over the remains of Byzantine and Crusader churches, encloses the rock where Jesus is said to have prayed. Some of the olive trees in the garden are many centuries old.

golgotha.name: Golgotha (Calvary)
golgotha.note: "The place of a skull" (Aramaic Golgotha, Latin Calvaria), outside the city wall but near it, beside a road. The rock of Calvary is enclosed in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built by Constantine from AD 326 over a site the Jerusalem church remembered. In AD 30 this was an old quarry just outside the city's second wall; the third wall of the AD 40s brought it inside. Some Protestants since the 1880s have preferred "Gordon's Calvary", a skull-shaped hill north of the Damascus Gate.

herodpalace.name: Herod Antipas' quarters in Jerusalem
herodpalace.note: Luke says only that Antipas was in Jerusalem for the feast. He probably lodged in the old Hasmonean palace, which Josephus places on the western hill of the Upper City, overlooking the Temple. It has not been excavated.

olives.name: Mount of Olives
olives.note: The ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, about 2,700 ft high. Constantine built the Eleona church over a cave near the summit; the Pater Noster church there today recalls the teaching of the Lord's Prayer.

praetorium.name: Praetorium (Pilate's headquarters)
praetorium.note: Where the Roman prefect judged when he came up for the feasts. Philo and Josephus show later governors using Herod the Great's palace on the western hill (by today's Jaffa Gate and Citadel), and most scholars now place Pilate's trial there. An older tradition puts it at the Antonia Fortress north of the Temple, where the Via Dolorosa begins; the Lithostrotos pavement and "Ecce Homo" arch shown there date from Hadrian's city in the 2nd century.

tomb.name: The Tomb (Holy Sepulchre)
tomb.note: John says the tomb was new, in a garden near the place of crucifixion. The rock-cut tomb honored since the 4th century lies a few dozen yards west of Calvary inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, under the small shrine called the Edicule; other 1st-century tombs survive in the same quarry. The Garden Tomb near Gordon's Calvary is a peaceful place of prayer, but archaeologists date it to the Iron Age, centuries before Jesus.

upperroom.name: Upper Room (Cenacle)
upperroom.note: The Gospels name only "a large upper room furnished" in the city. Since at least the 4th century, Christians have honored a site on Mount Zion, in the southwest of the old city, as the room of the Last Supper and of Pentecost. The present Gothic hall was built by the Crusaders and Franciscans in the 12th to 14th centuries. Robertson suggests it may have been the house of John Mark's mother (Acts 12:12).

events.title: Jesus arrives at Bethany
events.summary: Passover is near, and pilgrims crowd into Jerusalem early to purify themselves. They look for Jesus in the Temple and wonder if he will dare come, since the chief priests have ordered anyone who knows where he is to report it. Six days before the Passover, Jesus comes up from Jericho to Bethany, where he had raised Lazarus. Crowds come out to see both Jesus and Lazarus, and the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too.
events.stay: Bethany, with his friends Martha, Mary and Lazarus; he went back there each night of the week.
events.journey: About 15 miles, climbing some 3,400 ft from the Jordan Valley on the steep Roman road up through the Judean wilderness.

scripture.text: They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast?"
Six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.

When the great crowd of the Jews learned that he was there, they came, not only on account of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests planned to put Lazarus also to death, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.

art.medium: Pen and ink on paper
art.title: Valley of Jehoshaphat, Coming from Bethany
art.description: A bare, sweeping hillside falls into the Kidron (Jehoshaphat) Valley, with the walls of Jerusalem along the ridge at the upper left, as seen by a traveler on the road from Bethany.
art.significance: One of Tissot's pen-and-ink studies of the landscape of Palestine, drawn on his travels and used for the Life of Christ.
art.symbolism: This is the view Jesus and the pilgrims had each day of Passion Week, walking from Bethany over the Mount of Olives to the city.
art.impact: Tissot's on-the-spot drawings are a record of the land's terraces, roads and villages before modern building.

events.orderNote: John sets the supper and anointing at Bethany here (12:2–8), right after the arrival. Robertson thinks John mentions it early only because it is his last word on Bethany, and follows Mark, who places it on the Tuesday evening (§141). Robertson dates the week to AD 30, or AD 29 if John 5:1 was not a Passover.

events.title: The triumphal entry into Jerusalem
events.summary: Near Bethphage, Jesus sends two disciples to bring a colt that has never been ridden. He rides it down the Mount of Olives while the crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road and shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" When the Pharisees tell him to silence his disciples, he says the very stones would cry out. Seeing the city, he weeps over it and foretells its destruction. In the Temple he heals the blind and lame and accepts the children's praise, then goes back to Bethany for the night.
events.stay: He looked around the Temple and, as it was late, went out to Bethany with the Twelve (Mark 11:11).
events.journey: About 2 miles from Bethany over the Mount of Olives by Bethphage, down across the Kidron Valley and up into the Temple.

scripture.text: "Tell the daughter of Zion, Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on an ass, and on a colt, the foal of an ass."
And the crowds that went before him and that followed him shouted, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!"
And when he drew near and saw the city he wept over it, saying, "Would that even today you knew the things that make for peace! But now they are hid from your eyes.

echoes.note: "Lo, your king comes to you... humble and riding on an ass, on a colt the foal of an ass."
The pilgrim psalm of Passover: "Save us" (Hosanna) and "Blessed be he who enters in the name of the Lord!"

art.title: Entry into Jerusalem
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ rides a donkey toward the city gate, blessing, with the apostles behind him. Boys climb trees to cut branches, and townspeople spread their cloaks on the ground before him.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's fresco cycle of the life of Christ in the chapel built by Enrico Scrovegni, a turning point toward natural, weighty figures in Western painting.
art.symbolism: Christ moves steadily toward the gate on the right, the direction of the Passion scenes that follow on the chapel wall.
art.impact: The Scrovegni Chapel is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021) and one of the founding monuments of Renaissance painting.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Procession on the Mount of Olives
art.description: Seen from below, a crowd winds down a stony hillside path. Men carry palm branches and lay cloaks on the road as Jesus comes down on the colt.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The steep, rocky path and olive trees show the real descent from Bethphage toward the Kidron and the city.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Mark says Jesus only looked around the Temple on Sunday and cleansed it on Monday. Matthew and Luke tell the cleansing straight after the entry; Robertson follows Mark's more exact day-by-day order. Matthew alone mentions both an ass and her colt.

events.title: The barren fig tree cursed
events.summary: On Monday morning, walking in from Bethany, Jesus is hungry. He sees a fig tree in full leaf, but finds nothing on it but leaves, "for it was not the season for figs." He says that no one will ever eat fruit from it again, and the disciples hear him. It is an acted parable: a show of leaves without fruit, like the Temple religion he will confront the same morning.
events.stay: He spent the night at Bethany and walked back into the city in the morning.
events.journey: About a mile from Bethany up toward Bethphage on the road to Jerusalem.

scripture.text: And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.

echoes.note: "There are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree": the prophets' picture of a fruitless people.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Accursed Fig Tree
art.description: Jesus turns away from a large fig tree in full leaf beside a stone wall, one hand raised to his head. The disciples follow along the dusty road behind him.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The tree is thick with leaves but has no fruit: an image of outward show without the fruit God looks for.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Matthew tells the cursing and the withering together, as if in one morning (21:18–22). Mark spreads them over two days, with the Temple cleansing in between, and Robertson follows Mark. The exact place on the road is not known.

events.title: Jesus cleanses the Temple
events.summary: In the Temple courts Jesus drives out those who buy and sell, overturns the tables of the money-changers and the seats of the dove sellers, and will not let anyone carry goods through the Temple. Quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah, he says God's house is to be a house of prayer for all the nations, but they have made it a den of robbers. The chief priests and scribes look for a way to destroy him, but they fear him, because the people hang on his words.
events.journey: About a mile on from Bethphage down the Mount of Olives and into the Temple.

scripture.text: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons; and he would not allow any one to carry anything through the temple.
And he taught, and said to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers."

echoes.note: "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples."
"Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?"

art.title: Expulsion of the Money-changers from the Temple
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Before a Gothic temple facade, Christ raises a whip of cords at the traders. Tables are overturned, animals run, and two children shelter among the apostles, one clutching a dove.
art.significance: It follows the Entry into Jerusalem in Giotto's Passion sequence, as in Mark's order of the week.
art.symbolism: The frightened children seek safety with the disciples, while the priests gather at the right to plot: the cleansing sets the Passion in motion.
art.impact: One of the most reproduced images of the scene in Western art.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Jesus Forbids the Carrying of Loads in the Forecourt of the Temple
art.description: On the steps of a Temple gateway, Jesus in white turns back people carrying jars and bundles on their heads, who were using the courts as a shortcut.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: It illustrates a detail found only in Mark (11:16): Jesus would not let anyone carry goods through the Temple, treating even its outer court as holy ground.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: John tells of a cleansing at the first Passover of the ministry (John 2:13–22). Robertson, like many, holds that Jesus cleansed the Temple twice, at the start and the end; many other scholars think there was one cleansing, which John placed early for theological reasons.

events.title: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus
events.summary: Some Greeks who have come up to worship at the feast ask Philip, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus." Philip tells Andrew, and they tell Jesus. He answers that his hour has come: like a grain of wheat, he must die to bear much fruit. Troubled in soul, he prays "Father, glorify your name," and a voice answers from heaven. He says that when he is lifted up from the earth he will draw all to himself. John closes Jesus' public ministry with the people's unbelief and his last appeal to believe in the light.

scripture.text: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Beth-saida in Galilee, and said to him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.
and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to myself."

echoes.note: "Lord, who has believed our report?", quoted by John (12:38) of the people's unbelief.
The blinded eyes and hardened heart, also quoted in John 12:40.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Gentiles Ask to See Jesus
art.description: In a colonnade of the Temple overlooking the city, Jesus in white stands at the right while a disciple points him out to a group of strangers in foreign dress.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot sets the scene on the edge of the Temple, where Gentiles could come no further than the outer court.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Only John tells this, without naming the day. Robertson places it on the Monday in the Temple. The Greeks were probably Gentile God-fearers, who could pray only in the outer Court of the Gentiles.

events.title: The fig tree found withered
events.summary: Each evening Jesus leaves the city, and each morning the people come early to hear him in the Temple. On Tuesday morning, passing the same way, the disciples see the fig tree withered to its roots. Peter remembers and points it out. Jesus answers with a lesson on faith and prayer: whoever believes without doubting could tell a mountain to be cast into the sea. He adds that when they pray they must forgive.
events.stay: Luke says he spent the nights "on the mount called Olivet" (21:37), which includes Bethany on its eastern slope.
events.journey: About a mile from Bethany back up the road toward Bethphage.

scripture.text: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Master, look! The fig tree which you cursed has withered."

And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God. Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and cast into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Jesus Goes in the Evening to Bethany
art.description: Jesus walks down a stony path on the Mount of Olives with a disciple and some women behind him, the walls of Jerusalem rising across the valley.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: It pictures Mark 11:19, "when evening came they went out of the city": the daily walk between Jerusalem and Bethany on which the disciples saw the withered tree.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Matthew says the tree withered "at once" and tells it on the same morning as the curse. Mark has the disciples notice it the next morning. Robertson takes Mark's two-day account as the exact one.

events.title: "By what authority?"
events.summary: As Jesus walks in the Temple, a delegation of the Sanhedrin, chief priests, scribes and elders, demands to know by what authority he acts and who gave it to him. He answers with a question: was the baptism of John from heaven or from men? They dare not say "from heaven," nor "from men," since the people hold John to be a prophet. When they answer "We do not know," Jesus refuses to tell them. It opens a long day of debate in the Temple courts.
events.journey: About a mile on from Bethphage into the Temple.

scripture.text: and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
Was the baptism of John from heaven or from men? Answer me."

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Chief Priests Ask Jesus by What Right Does He Act in This Way
art.description: Jesus, in white, raises a finger as he answers a group of elders and priests leaning on a low wall, while a crowd presses in behind them.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The barrier between Jesus and the rulers shows the line drawn on this day of controversy.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Robertson calls Tuesday "a day of controversy": the leaders formally test Jesus' standing as a teacher, as they had the right to do, and he answers with three parables (the two sons, the wicked tenants, the wedding feast).

events.title: The parable of the two sons
events.summary: A man asks his two sons to work in his vineyard. The first says no, but later repents and goes. The second says "I go, sir," but does not go. Jesus asks which did his father's will, and the leaders answer, the first. He tells them that tax collectors and harlots, who believed John, are going into the kingdom of God before them.

scripture.text: "What do you think? A man had two sons; and he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.' And he answered, 'I will not'; but afterward he repented and went. And he went to the second and said the same; and he answered, 'I go, sir,' but did not go.
Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.

art.medium: Pen and ink on paper
art.title: Vineyards with Their Watch Towers
art.description: Terraced vineyards of bare vines, enclosed by dry-stone walls, climb a hillside toward two round stone watchtowers.
art.significance: One of Tissot's pen-and-ink studies of the landscape of Palestine, drawn on his travels and used for the Life of Christ.
art.symbolism: The walls and towers are the ones Jesus describes in his vineyard parables (Matthew 21:33): the setting of the two sons sent to work in their father's vineyard.
art.impact: Tissot's on-the-spot drawings are a record of the land's terraces, roads and villages before modern building.

events.title: The parable of the wicked tenants
people: The chief priests, scribes and Pharisees
events.summary: A man plants a vineyard, lets it out to tenants and goes away. When he sends servants for his share of the fruit, the tenants beat and kill them. Last of all he sends his beloved son, and they kill him too, hoping to seize the inheritance. Jesus quotes the psalm of the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone. The leaders see that he has told the parable against them and want to arrest him, but they fear the crowd.

scripture.text: He had still one other, a beloved son; finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.'
Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the scriptures: 'The very stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?

echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: "the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel."
"The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner."

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Son of the Vineyard
art.description: The owner's son lies dead on a heap of stones outside a walled vineyard, while the tenants run off across the terraces below the watchtowers.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot paints the parable's climax, "they took him and killed him, and cast him out of the vineyard" (Mark 12:8), as a foreshadowing of Christ's own death outside the city.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.title: The parable of the wedding feast
events.summary: A king gives a marriage feast for his son, but the invited guests refuse to come; some mock and even kill his servants. The king sends his servants into the streets to bring in all they find, good and bad, until the hall is full. One guest is found without a wedding garment and is cast out. "Many are called, but few are chosen."

scripture.text: "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a marriage feast for his son,

Go therefore to the thoroughfares, and invite to the marriage feast as many as you find.' And those servants went out into the streets and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good; so the wedding hall was filled with guests.
For many are called, but few are chosen."

echoes.note: The Lord's feast for all peoples on his holy mountain.

art.credit: Photo: Didier Descouens, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
art.title: The Parable of the Wedding Feast (detail)
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: In this detail, the king, in a gold mantle and a heavy chain, flings out his arm in command, while an old servant at his side looks up at him.
art.significance: Strozzi, a Genoese Capuchin friar turned painter, worked in Venice from about 1633, and his loose, rich brushwork helped renew Venetian painting.
art.symbolism: The king's outstretched hand sends his servants out to the thoroughfares to gather guests, good and bad.
art.impact: A fine example of Strozzi's late Venetian style, influenced by Veronese.

events.orderNote: Luke's parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:16–24) is similar, but it is set at a Pharisee's dinner earlier in the journey; Robertson treats the two as different parables.

events.title: Tribute to Caesar
events.summary: The Pharisees send some of their disciples with the Herodians to trap Jesus: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? A yes would anger the people, a no would mark him as a rebel against Rome. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose likeness and inscription it bears. "Caesar's," they say. "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." They are amazed and fall silent.

scripture.text: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they were amazed at him.

art.title: The Tribute Money
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: A grey-bearded man in a rough shoulder cloth holds up a small coin to Christ, who looks back calmly and points upward with one finger.
art.significance: A late work signed TITIANVS F., painted when Titian was in his seventies. He had painted the same subject about fifty years earlier (Gemäldegalerie, Dresden).
art.symbolism: Christ's raised finger points beyond the coin to God, to whom the things that are God's belong.
art.impact: Titian's two versions made the half-length 'Tribute Money' a favorite subject for later Venetian and Baroque painters.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Tribute Money
art.description: On the steps of a Temple portico, Jesus in white looks down at a coin held out to him by a man in a turban, surrounded by curious elders and scholars.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The crowd of questioners pressing around Jesus shows the trap being sprung in public, before many witnesses.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.history: The coin was a denarius, the Roman silver coin of a day's wage. Under Tiberius it carried his portrait and the inscription TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, "Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus."

events.title: The Sadducees and the resurrection
events.summary: The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring a puzzle: a woman married seven brothers in turn under the law of levirate marriage. Whose wife will she be in the resurrection? Jesus says they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. In the resurrection people do not marry but are like angels. And God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: he is not God of the dead, but of the living.

scripture.text: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God said to him, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong."
Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living; for all live to him."

echoes.note: God at the burning bush: "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob."
The law that a brother should marry his dead brother's widow, on which the puzzle rests.

events.orderNote: Robertson thinks this was probably a stock riddle the Sadducees had often used against the Pharisees.

events.title: The great commandment
events.summary: Hearing that Jesus has silenced the Sadducees, a scribe asks him which commandment is the first of all. Jesus answers with the Shema: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength. The second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. The scribe agrees that this is more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. Jesus tells him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God," and after that no one dares ask him any question.

scripture.text: Jesus answered, "The first is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.' The second is this, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."

echoes.note: The Shema, prayed daily: "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God is one Lord."
"You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

events.orderNote: Matthew presents the question as a test; Mark shows the scribe as sincere and praised by Jesus. Luke has a similar exchange with a lawyer much earlier, before the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–28).

events.title: Whose son is the Christ?
events.summary: Now Jesus asks the question. The scribes say the Christ is the son of David. Yet David, inspired by the Holy Spirit, calls him "my Lord" in Psalm 110. How then can he be David's son? No one can answer him a word, and the great crowd hears him gladly. The riddle points to a Messiah who is more than a royal descendant.

scripture.text: David himself, inspired by the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, till I put your enemies under your feet.' David himself calls him Lord; so how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.

echoes.note: "The Lord says to my lord: 'Sit at my right hand.'" The Old Testament verse most often quoted in the New.

events.title: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees
events.summary: In his last public discourse, Jesus warns the crowds and his disciples against the scribes and Pharisees: do what they teach, but not what they do. They love the places of honor and long robes, and devour widows' houses. Then come seven woes against their hypocrisy: they tithe mint and dill but neglect justice, mercy and faith, and are like whitewashed tombs. He ends with a lament over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets, and whose children he would have gathered as a hen gathers her brood.

scripture.text: He who is greatest among you shall be your servant; whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
"Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within they are full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness.

"O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killing the prophets and stoning those who are sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not!

echoes.note: The stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada in the Temple court, the last murder of a prophet in the Hebrew Bible's order (Matthew 23:35).

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Woe unto You, Scribes and Pharisees
art.description: In a colonnade of the Temple, Jesus strides forward with his arm raised in denunciation, while scribes and Pharisees sit hunched on benches, hiding their faces.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The seated teachers on their benches recall "Moses' seat" (Matthew 23:2), the place of authority they have used for themselves.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Jerusalem, Jerusalem
art.description: Seen from behind, Jesus stands in a Temple court with arms spread wide over a great crowd seated on the pavement, the city rising beyond the walls.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: His open arms echo the lament's image of a hen gathering her brood under her wings (Matthew 23:37).
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Luke gives similar woes at a Pharisee's table in Galilee or Perea (Luke 11:37–54), and the lament over Jerusalem earlier on the journey (Luke 13:34–35). Robertson holds that Jesus spoke such words more than once; others think Matthew gathered them here.

events.title: The widow's mite
events.summary: Jesus sits opposite the treasury and watches people put in their gifts. Many rich people put in large sums. A poor widow puts in two copper coins, worth about a penny. Jesus calls his disciples and tells them she has given more than all the rest, for they gave from their abundance, but she out of her poverty gave everything she had. Robertson notes it is Jesus' last scene in the Temple.

scripture.text: And he called his disciples to him, and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury. For they all contributed out of their abundance; but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, her whole living."

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Widow's Mite
art.description: A poor woman in a plain grey mantle walks away from the Temple treasury carrying a child, while Jesus, seated with his disciples by the doorway, points her out to them.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: A richly dressed man strides out of the same door behind her: the contrast is the whole lesson.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.history: The "treasury" was probably the thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women, described in the Mishnah (Shekalim 6.5). The widow's coins were lepta, the smallest bronze coins in circulation.

events.title: The Olivet discourse
events.summary: As they leave the Temple, a disciple admires its huge stones. Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. Sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew ask him privately when this will be. He warns of false messiahs, wars, persecution and the desolating sacrilege, and tells them to flee Judea when they see Jerusalem surrounded. Then the Son of man will come on the clouds with power and glory. No one knows the day or the hour, so they must watch.
events.journey: Under a mile: out of the Temple, across the Kidron Valley and up the slope of the Mount of Olives.

scripture.text: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another, that will not be thrown down."
And then they will see the Son of man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. "But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. Take heed, watch and pray; for you do not know when the time will come.

echoes.note: "One like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven and given an everlasting kingdom.
The "abomination that makes desolate" (Mark 13:14).

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Prophecy of the Destruction of the Temple
art.description: Under a large tree on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sits with his head in his hand, four disciples around him, facing the massive walls of the Temple across the valley.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The great walls he foretells will be thrown down fill the whole background, solid and seemingly permanent.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Disciples Admire the Buildings of the Temple
art.description: Coming down a broad stairway of the Temple, the disciples gesture with excitement at the buildings around them while Jesus walks among them, eyes lowered.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Their wonder at "what wonderful stones" (Mark 13:1) meets his silence, just before the prophecy.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.history: The Romans under Titus took Jerusalem and burned the Temple in AD 70, about forty years later. Huge Herodian stones thrown down from the Temple Mount still lie on the 1st-century street below the Western Wall.
events.orderNote: How much of the discourse refers to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and how much to the end of the age is much debated. Robertson sees the city's destruction as a symbol of the end and warns against pressing details of time. Luke sets this teaching in the Temple (21:5–7); Mark and Matthew on the Mount of Olives.

events.title: The parable of the ten virgins
events.summary: Ten maidens take their lamps to meet the bridegroom. Five wise ones bring extra oil; five foolish ones do not. The bridegroom is delayed and they all fall asleep. At midnight comes the cry that he is here, and the foolish find their lamps going out. While they go to buy oil the door is shut. "Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour."

scripture.text: And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast; and the door was shut.
Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Wise Virgins
art.description: Five young women in white sit asleep against a stone wall hung with garlands, waiting for the bridegroom. Their small oil lamps still burn on the petal-strewn floor.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Their lamps stay lit even as they sleep: the oil they brought stands for a readiness that does not run out.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Foolish Virgins
art.description: In the dark, the foolish virgins run in a windblown line, holding up empty lamps and oil jars as they hurry to buy oil.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The dark night and the rush of figures stress how suddenly the bridegroom comes and how late they are.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.title: The parable of the talents
events.summary: A man going on a journey entrusts his property to three servants: five talents, two talents and one, each according to his ability. The first two trade and double what they were given. The third buries his talent in the ground. When the master returns, he praises the faithful servants and takes the talent from the one who hid it out of fear. A talent was a very large sum, many years' wages.

scripture.text: His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant; you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your master.'
For to every one who has will more be given, and he will have abundance; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

art.title: The Parable of the Talents
art.medium: Oil painting
art.description: In a lofty hall, a servant leans over a table to lay out his coins before his richly robed master, while other servants wait their turn.
art.significance: De Poorter was a Haarlem painter in the circle of Rembrandt, known for small, finely lit biblical scenes.
art.symbolism: The shaft of light across the floor and the master's open hand stress the moment of reckoning when the master returns.
art.impact: Shows how Dutch painters of the 1600s read the parable as a story about honest stewardship and accounting.

events.orderNote: Luke's parable of the pounds (Luke 19:11–27), told near Jericho a few days earlier, is similar. Robertson treats them as two different parables.

events.title: The sheep and the goats
events.summary: Jesus closes the discourse with the Last Judgment. The Son of man comes in glory with his angels and sits on his throne, and all the nations are gathered before him. He separates them as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. Those who fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked and visited the sick and imprisoned did it to him, and inherit the kingdom.

scripture.text: "When the Son of man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate them one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,
And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me.'

echoes.note: "I judge between sheep and sheep, rams and he-goats."

art.title: The Last Judgment
art.medium: Tempera on panel
art.description: Christ sits in judgment in a ring of angels, with saints ranged on either side. Below, a road of open tombs divides the blessed, dancing with angels in a garden at left, from the damned driven by demons into hell at right.
art.significance: Painted for the Camaldolese monastery of Santa Maria degli Angeli in Florence, early in Fra Angelico's career.
art.symbolism: The division at right and left follows Matthew 25: the sheep on the King's right hand, the goats on his left.
art.impact: The ring dance of the blessed with angels is one of the most loved images of heaven in Italian art.

events.title: The plot to kill Jesus
events.summary: When he has finished these sayings, Jesus tells his disciples that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified. Meanwhile the chief priests and elders gather in the palace of the high priest Caiaphas. They take counsel to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him, but not during the feast, for fear of a riot among the people.
events.stay: Robertson thinks Jesus spent Tuesday night and the quiet Wednesday with the disciples at Bethany.
events.journey: About 1.5 miles back over the Mount of Olives to Bethany.

scripture.text: "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified."
Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Conspiracy of the Jews
art.description: A huddle of elderly priests and elders in turbans and heavy robes confer in low voices in a dim hall behind an iron grille.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot shows the council as a closed circle in shadow, plotting "by stealth" (Matthew 26:4).
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Robertson places Jesus' prediction at Bethany on Tuesday evening, which by Jewish reckoning was already Wednesday, "two days" before the Passover. The council itself met in Jerusalem at Caiaphas' house. The Gospels record nothing of Wednesday; Robertson takes it as a day of rest in Bethany.

events.title: Mary anoints Jesus at Bethany
events.summary: At a supper in the house of Simon the leper, Martha serves and Lazarus is at table. Mary breaks an alabaster flask of costly nard and pours it over Jesus' head and feet, wiping his feet with her hair, and the house fills with the fragrance. Some, Judas loudest of all, complain that it could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor. Jesus defends her: she has anointed his body beforehand for burial. Wherever the gospel is preached, what she has done will be told in memory of her.

scripture.text: Mary took a pound of costly ointment of pure nard and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burying. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Ointment of the Magdalene
art.description: Jesus reclines on a cushioned couch in a garden courtyard while a woman, her long hair loose, bends over his feet. The other guests lean forward from the table, some startled, some disapproving.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot follows the Western tradition that identified Mary of Bethany with Mary Magdalene, hence the title. The guests' reactions echo the complaint about waste in John 12:4–5.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: John places the supper six days before the Passover; Mark and Matthew two days before. Robertson follows Mark. Mark and Matthew say "a woman"; John names Mary. Robertson insists it is a different event from the anointing by a sinful woman in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50), though Western tradition long identified Mary of Bethany with that woman and with Mary Magdalene.

events.title: Judas agrees to betray Jesus
events.summary: Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests and asks what they will give him to hand Jesus over. Luke says Satan entered into him. The priests are glad and agree to pay him thirty pieces of silver. From then on he looks for an opportunity to betray Jesus to them away from the crowds.

scripture.text: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, "What will you give me if I deliver him to you?" And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him.

echoes.note: The shepherd's wages, "thirty shekels of silver," thrown to the potter in the house of the Lord.
Thirty shekels of silver: the price paid for a slave.

art.title: The Pact of Judas
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Judas, in a yellow cloak, takes the money bag from the priests beside a small open loggia. A black devil stands behind him with a hand on his shoulder.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel, a turning point in Western painting toward weight, space and human feeling.
art.symbolism: Judas's yellow robe became the traditional color of betrayal; the devil at his back shows Luke's words that Satan entered into him.
art.impact: The Scrovegni frescoes are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and among the most studied paintings of the Middle Ages.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Judas Goes to Find the Jews
art.description: Judas, wrapped in a dark cloak, walks away from a carved balustrade where a crowd of elders leans over, listening to a pleading man.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot isolates Judas in the foreground, his face closed and downcast, already apart from the Twelve.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Robertson links the bargain to the anointing: Judas, "stung by the rebuke" at the feast, goes to the rulers that same night. Matthew and Mark tell it straight after the anointing; Luke after the council's plot.

events.title: Preparing the Passover
people: A man carrying a jar of water
events.summary: On the day when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, Jesus sends Peter and John into the city. A man carrying a jar of water, an unusual sight, since women usually carried water, will lead them to a house. Its owner will show them a large upper room, furnished and ready. They find it as he told them and prepare the Passover: the lamb sacrificed in the Temple that afternoon, the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs and the wine.
events.stay: The upper room of a friend's house in Jerusalem; Robertson suggests the home of John Mark's parents.
events.journey: About 2 miles from Bethany over the Mount of Olives and across the Kidron into the city.

scripture.text: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, "Go and prepare the passover for us, that we may eat it."
And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us."

echoes.note: The first Passover: the lamb without blemish, its blood on the doorposts, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Man Bearing a Pitcher
art.description: Two disciples, Peter and John, pause beneath the high walls of Jerusalem and watch a man carrying a large water jar on his shoulder up a stepped street.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: The water carrier is the sign Jesus gave them (Mark 14:13); a man carrying water would have stood out, since it was usually women's work.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: The Synoptics present the Last Supper as the Passover meal, and Robertson agrees. John seems to place the slaying of the Passover lambs on Friday, as Jesus was dying (John 18:28; 19:14). Scholars explain this in several ways, among them a different calendar used by some Jews, or a Passover meal held a day early.

events.title: The Last Supper begins
events.summary: When the hour comes, Jesus reclines at table with the Twelve. He tells them he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with them before he suffers. A dispute breaks out over which of them is the greatest. Jesus tells them that among the Gentiles kings lord it over others, but among them the greatest must be as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves, "I am among you as one who serves." He promises them a kingdom and thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel.
events.stay: The upper room in Jerusalem, from sunset on Thursday, the start of the Jewish Friday.

scripture.text: And he said to them, "I have earnestly desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer; for I tell you I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God."

But not so with you; rather let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For which is the greater, one who sits at table, or one who serves? Is it not the one who sits at table? But I am among you as one who serves.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Last Supper (The Legal Passover)
art.description: Jesus and the apostles stand around a table draped in white, staffs in hand and cloaks over their heads, in a room hung with garlands.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot shows the Passover eaten as Exodus 12:11 commands, standing "with your loins girded... and your staff in your hand." His French title calls it the legal Passover meal.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

art.title: The Last Supper
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ and the Twelve sit at a long table under an open loggia. John leans against Jesus' breast, and Judas, at his side, reaches into the same dish.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's Passion cycle; the apostles seen from behind invite the viewer to sit at the table with them.
art.symbolism: The halos of the apostles have darkened with age; Judas's is painted dark on purpose, marking the betrayer.
art.impact: An early landmark in the long Italian tradition of Last Supper paintings that culminates in Leonardo.

events.orderNote: Luke tells the dispute after the supper (22:24–30). Robertson places it at the start of the meal, perhaps a quarrel over places at table, which would also explain the foot washing that follows.

events.title: Jesus washes the disciples' feet
events.summary: Knowing that his hour has come, and having loved his own, Jesus loves them to the end. During supper he rises, lays aside his garments, ties a towel around himself and washes the disciples' feet, a slave's task. Peter protests, "You shall never wash my feet," until Jesus tells him that unless he is washed he has no part in him. Jesus then tells them that he has given them an example: as he has done, so they must do to one another.

scripture.text: Then he poured water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.
Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no part in me."
If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done to you.

echoes.note: "He who ate of my bread has lifted his heel against me," quoted by Jesus here of his betrayer (John 13:18).

art.title: Jesus Washing Peter's Feet
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ kneels on the floor, a towel tied at his waist, washing Peter's feet in a copper basin. Peter sits with hands clasped and head bowed, while the other apostles crowd around the table to watch.
art.significance: Brown, close to the Pre-Raphaelites, first painted Christ bare-chested; critics objected, and he repainted him clothed.
art.symbolism: The Lord on his knees below the seated disciple turns the order of master and servant upside down (John 13:14–15).
art.impact: Its frank, physical realism made it one of the most discussed religious paintings of Victorian England.

art.title: Washing of the Feet
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Christ kneels before Peter, who raises a hand in protest, while the other apostles wait their turn; one at the left unties his sandal, another holds the water jug.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's Passion cycle, set in the same open room as his Last Supper next to it.
art.symbolism: Christ's halo is lower than the apostles' heads: the Master has taken the servant's place.
art.impact: A model for the many images of the Mandatum that later decorated church and monastery walls.

events.orderNote: Only John tells the foot washing, and he does not describe the institution of the Eucharist. The Church re-enacts the washing in the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday.

events.title: "One of you will betray me"
events.summary: Troubled in spirit, Jesus says, "One of you will betray me." The disciples are deeply grieved and ask one after another, "Is it I?" Peter signals to the beloved disciple, reclining next to Jesus, to ask whom he means. Jesus says it is the one to whom he gives the morsel after dipping it, and gives it to Judas. Satan enters Judas, and Jesus tells him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Judas goes out at once, "and it was night."

scripture.text: And as they were at table eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful, and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?"
Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I shall give this morsel when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
So, after receiving the morsel, he immediately went out; and it was night.

art.title: The Last Supper
art.medium: Tempera and oil on plaster
art.location: Refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan
art.description: Christ sits calmly at the center of a long table as the apostles recoil in groups of three at his words, "One of you will betray me." Judas, clutching a money bag, leans back into shadow.
art.significance: Painted for the Dominican friars' dining hall at the request of Duke Ludovico Sforza. Leonardo's experimental technique began to flake within his lifetime.
art.symbolism: Christ's head is framed by the bright central window and is the vanishing point of the whole room, so every line leads to him.
art.impact: Perhaps the most reproduced religious painting in the world. With the church, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: Judas Leaves the Cenacle
art.description: Judas, wrapped in a heavy brown cloak, slips out of a dark doorway into the cold light of the night street, looking back over his shoulder.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: It pictures John 13:30, "he immediately went out; and it was night": light behind him in the room, darkness ahead.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Luke places the warning about the betrayer after the bread and cup (22:21–23), which suggests Judas was present at the institution. Robertson follows Mark and John and places Judas's departure first.

events.title: The new commandment and the warning to Peter
events.summary: After Judas leaves, Jesus says the Son of man is now glorified. He gives them a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. He warns that they will all fall away this night, as Zechariah foretold. Peter protests that even if all fall away, he will not, and that he will die with him. Jesus tells him that before the cock crows twice, he will deny him three times. Yet he has prayed that Peter's faith may not fail, and once he has turned again, he must strengthen his brethren.

scripture.text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another; even as I have loved you, that you also love one another. By this all men will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another."

"Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren."
And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I say to you, this very night, before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times."

echoes.note: "Strike the shepherd, that the sheep may be scattered" (Mark 14:27).

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Protestations of Saint Peter
art.description: On a rocky path in the dark outside the city walls, Peter turns to Jesus with his hand raised, protesting his loyalty, as the other disciples walk on in silence.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot follows Mark and Matthew, who set the warning on the way to the Mount of Olives; a stair climbs the dark valley behind them.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Luke and John place the warning to Peter in the upper room; Mark and Matthew on the way to the Mount of Olives after the hymn. Robertson harmonizes them in one section; some think Jesus warned Peter twice. Only Mark has the cock crowing twice.

events.title: The institution of the Eucharist
events.summary: As they are eating, Jesus takes bread, blesses and breaks it, and gives it to the disciples, saying, "Take, eat; this is my body." Then he takes the cup, gives thanks, and gives it to them: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins." He commands them, "Do this in remembrance of me." The Church has always received these words as the institution of the Holy Eucharist: the gift of his Body and Blood, given the night before he offered himself on the Cross, and the beginning of the ministerial priesthood of the apostles. St Paul hands on the same words as a tradition he received from the Lord.

scripture.text: Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed, and broke it, and gave it to the disciples and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, "Drink of it, all of you; for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.
And he took bread, and when he had given thanks he broke it and gave it to them, saying, "This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me."
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.

echoes.note: Moses seals the covenant at Sinai: "Behold the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you."
The promised new covenant, written on the heart.

art.title: Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament: The Last Supper
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: In a calm Flemish hall, Christ sits at the center of a square table and raises his hand in blessing over a single Host above the chalice. The apostles sit in stillness around him, and four men in contemporary dress look on.
art.significance: Commissioned by the Confraternity of the Holy Sacrament in Leuven, whose contract specified the subjects. It is among the first Netherlandish paintings to show Christ consecrating the Host rather than naming the betrayer.
art.symbolism: Christ holds the Host where a priest holds it at Mass, so the Last Supper is shown as the first Eucharist. The onlookers are thought to be members of the confraternity, or Bouts himself.
art.impact: A landmark of early Netherlandish painting and one of the earliest northern works to use a single vanishing point for the room.

art.title: Institution of the Eucharist (Communion of the Apostles)
art.medium: Fresco
art.location: Cell 35, Convent of San Marco, Florence
art.description: Christ moves along the table giving Communion to the apostles with his own hand. Some sit, some kneel, and the Virgin Mary kneels in prayer at the left.
art.significance: Painted for a friar's cell in the Dominican convent of San Marco, as an aid to prayer.
art.symbolism: The scene looks like a Mass: Christ holds a paten and chalice and gives the Host as a priest does, and the kneeling apostles mirror the friars receiving Communion.
art.impact: A classic image of the Eucharist as Christ's own gift, often reproduced in First Communion books.

events.orderNote: Mark and Matthew give one account and Paul (1 Corinthians, about AD 56, the earliest written) and Luke another. Luke mentions a cup before the bread (22:17) and the cup of the covenant after supper (22:20). Robertson follows Mark's order and places the institution after Judas has gone out; Luke's order suggests Judas was still present.

events.title: The farewell discourse
events.summary: Jesus comforts his troubled disciples. In his Father's house are many rooms, and he goes to prepare a place for them. When Thomas asks the way, he answers, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Philip asks to see the Father, and Jesus says that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Counselor, the Holy Spirit, who will teach them all things, and he leaves them his peace.

scripture.text: In my Father's house are many rooms; if it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And when I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also.
Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father, but by me.
Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.

art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.title: The Last Sermon of Our Lord
art.description: In the upper room, hung with red curtains, Jesus stands in the center holding a long white cloth, while the apostles stand in two rows facing him, hands joined in prayer.
art.significance: One of about 350 watercolors in Tissot's Life of Christ, painted after his journeys to Palestine in 1886–87 and 1889.
art.symbolism: Tissot's title names the farewell discourse of John 14–17, Jesus' last teaching before the Passion.
art.impact: Shown in Paris in 1894 and bought by the Brooklyn Museum in 1900; the series shaped how a generation pictured the Gospel world.

events.orderNote: Robertson reads John 13–17 as one whole: dialogue in the upper room, then a monologue, then the prayer. Jesus ends chapter 14 with "Rise, let us go hence," so the following chapters may have been spoken on the way.

events.title: The true vine
events.summary: "I am the vine, you are the branches." Jesus tells his disciples to abide in him and in his love, for apart from him they can do nothing. No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends, and he calls them friends, not servants. He warns that the world will hate them as it hated him. He promises that the Spirit of truth will come, and that their sorrow will turn to joy. "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world."

scripture.text: I am the vine, you are the branches. He who abides in me, and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
I have said this to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world."

echoes.note: Israel as the vine God brought out of Egypt and planted.

art.title: Christ the True Vine
art.medium: Tempera and gold on panel
art.description: Christ sits at the center of a vine growing from one trunk, holding an open Gospel book. The twelve apostles sit on its branches among grape clusters, each with a book or scroll.
art.significance: A classic Byzantine and post-Byzantine icon type, made in Crete for Orthodox and Catholic patrons alike.
art.symbolism: The open book carries the words of John 15: "I am the vine, you are the branches." The apostles grow from Christ and bear fruit only in him.
art.impact: One of the most widely reproduced icons of the subject.

events.orderNote: Robertson suggests this was spoken "possibly on the street," after they left the upper room at the end of John 14 and sang the hymn. Others think Jesus spoke it before leaving the room; John 18:1 says he went out only after the prayer of chapter 17.

events.title: The high priestly prayer
events.summary: Lifting up his eyes to heaven, Jesus prays: "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son." He prays for his disciples, whom the Father gave him out of the world, that they may be kept from the evil one and consecrated in the truth. He prays also for all who will believe through their word, that they may all be one, as he and the Father are one, so that the world may believe. Robertson calls it "the real Lord's Prayer."

scripture.text: And this is eternal life, that they know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

"I do not pray for these only, but also for those who believe in me through their word, that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.

events.orderNote: Robertson suggests Jesus prayed this "possibly near Gethsemane." John 18:1 says that after these words he went out across the Kidron, so many place it in the upper room or in the city.

events.title: The agony in Gethsemane
events.summary: After singing a hymn, they go out across the Kidron to a garden called Gethsemane. Jesus takes Peter, James and John with him, saying his soul is very sorrowful, even to death. He falls on the ground and prays that the cup may pass from him, "yet not what I will, but what you will." Luke tells of an angel strengthening him and of sweat like great drops of blood. Three times he returns and finds the disciples asleep. At last he rouses them: the hour has come, and the betrayer is at hand.
events.journey: About a mile from the upper room down through the city and across the Kidron Valley to the foot of the Mount of Olives.

scripture.text: And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will."
And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down upon the ground.
Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."

echoes.note: The cup of the Lord's wrath, drunk to the dregs.
David, betrayed by his counselor, crosses the Kidron and goes up the Mount of Olives weeping.

art.title: The Agony in the Garden
art.medium: Egg tempera on panel
art.description: Christ kneels in prayer on a rocky outcrop at dawn while Peter, James and John sleep below. A small angel holds out a chalice in the sky, and Judas leads the soldiers along the road across the valley.
art.significance: An early work by Bellini, closely modeled on Mantegna's version of the same subject; the two now hang in the same London gallery.
art.symbolism: The chalice answers Christ's prayer, "remove this cup from me" (Mark 14:36); the dawn light already announces the day of the Passion.
art.impact: Celebrated as one of the first Italian paintings to make light and landscape carry the emotion of the scene.

art.title: The Agony in the Garden
art.medium: Egg tempera on panel
art.description: Christ kneels on a rock ledge before a group of child angels holding the instruments of the Passion. The three apostles sleep in the foreground, and Judas and the soldiers come out of a walled Jerusalem behind.
art.significance: Painted by Bellini's brother-in-law; Bellini knew it and made his own version.
art.symbolism: A vulture on a dead tree waits as an omen of death, while the angels show the cross and column of the coming Passion.
art.impact: With Bellini's picture, a famous paired case study in how two Renaissance masters treated one subject.

events.orderNote: Luke 22:43–44 (the angel and the bloody sweat) is missing from some early manuscripts but is in many others and in the Church's text. Robertson places the agony late in the night, at the start of the Jewish Friday.

events.title: The betrayal and arrest
events.summary: While Jesus is still speaking, Judas arrives with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests, together with a band of soldiers. He greets Jesus with a kiss, the agreed sign. When Jesus says "I am he," they draw back and fall to the ground. Peter cuts off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's slave, but Jesus heals him and goes willingly. All the disciples forsake him and flee; Mark alone adds a young man who escapes, leaving his linen cloth behind.

scripture.text: but Jesus said to him, "Judas, would you betray the Son of man with a kiss?"
Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?"
And they all forsook him, and fled.

echoes.note: "Strike the shepherd, that the sheep may be scattered," which Jesus quoted that same night (Mark 14:27).
Joab kisses Amasa in greeting and kills him: the treacherous kiss.

art.title: The Arrest of Christ (Kiss of Judas)
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Judas wraps Christ in his yellow cloak to kiss him. The two faces meet in profile at the center, surrounded by soldiers, torches, clubs and spears. At left Peter cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant.
art.significance: Part of Giotto's cycle of the lives of Mary and Christ, painted for Enrico Scrovegni's private chapel. It is one of the most famous images of the Passion.
art.symbolism: Christ's calm, steady gaze meets Judas' coarse, ape-like profile: the moment good and evil look each other in the face. Judas' cloak swallows Christ, as betrayal tries to swallow him.
art.impact: The Scrovegni frescoes mark the birth of a new, human and dramatic style in Western painting; this scene is often reproduced as its high point.

art.title: The Taking of Christ
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.location: National Gallery of Ireland, Dublin (on loan from the Jesuit Community)
art.description: In a tight, dark frieze of figures, Judas presses his kiss on Christ as armored soldiers seize him. Christ's hands are folded in quiet surrender. At left a disciple flees screaming; at right a man holds up a lantern.
art.significance: Painted in Rome for the Marchese Ciriaco Mattei. It was lost for two centuries and rediscovered in 1990 hanging in the Jesuit house in Dublin.
art.symbolism: The man with the lantern at far right is generally taken to be Caravaggio himself: like the viewer, he looks on and holds a little light to the scene. The fleeing disciple at left is often linked to the young man of Mark 14:51–52.
art.impact: Its rediscovery was a sensation in the art world, and it is now one of the best-known Caravaggios outside Italy.

events.orderNote: Only Luke records the healing of the ear, and only John names Peter and Malchus. Many readers since early times have guessed that the young man of Mark 14:51–52 was Mark himself, but the Gospel does not say.

events.title: Jesus before Annas
events.summary: The arresting party binds Jesus and leads him first to Annas, father-in-law of the reigning high priest Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest himself (AD 6–15) and five of his sons held the office after him, so he still wielded great power. He questions Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answers that he has taught openly, and when an officer strikes him he calmly asks why.
events.journey: About 1 mile: back across the Kidron Valley and up into the Upper City. Tradition follows the ancient stepped street that climbs to St Peter in Gallicantu.

scripture.text: First they led him to Annas; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.
Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together; I have said nothing secretly.
Jesus answered him, "If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?"

art.title: The Tribunal of Annas
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Guards drag Jesus by his robe through a pillared hall, away from the raised seat where Annas and the elders sit. A crowd of servants raise their fists behind him.
art.significance: Part of Tissot's 350-picture Life of Christ, painted after long study trips to Palestine in the 1880s.
art.symbolism: The light falls on the white-robed Christ in the middle of a rough, shadowed crowd; the high priests sit apart, high and remote.
art.impact: Shows how the night hearing may have looked: a large priestly house, armed retainers and a hurried, violent handling of the prisoner.

events.orderNote: Only John records this hearing. Robertson counts it as the first of three stages of the Jewish trial: Annas, then an informal night session before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin, then the formal sentence at dawn. John calls Annas "the high priest" here (18:19), as the Jews still did.

events.date: Before dawn Friday, Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: The trial before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin
people: The chief priests, elders and scribes
events.summary: Annas sends Jesus bound to Caiaphas, where the council has gathered by night. Many false witnesses come forward, but their stories do not agree. Jesus stays silent until the high priest puts him under oath: is he the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? Jesus answers "I am" and speaks of the Son of man seated at the right hand of Power. Caiaphas tears his robe, the council judges him deserving of death, and they spit on him, blindfold him and strike him.

scripture.text: But he was silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am; and you will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
And some began to spit on him, and to cover his face, and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.

echoes.note: "One like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom.
The servant gives his back to the smiters and does not hide his face from shame and spitting.

art.title: Christ before Caiaphas
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: At night, in a plain room lit by a single torch, Caiaphas tears open his robe on his seat while Annas sits beside him. Jesus stands before them held by guards, and a man raises his hand to strike him.
art.significance: The scene follows the Arrest in Giotto's Passion cycle in the Scrovegni Chapel.
art.symbolism: The torch on the wall marks the hour of darkness. Caiaphas' torn robe and the raised hand contrast with Christ's quiet, upright stance.
