art.impact: Part of the fresco cycle that shaped the way Western art tells the Passion as human drama.

art.title: The Torn Cloak: Jesus Condemned to Death
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a lamplit hall packed to the walls, the high priest stands on a raised seat at right and rips the neck of his robe with both hands. Council members in the dark foreground raise their arms, and across the room Jesus stands bound among the guards.
art.significance: Tissot imagines the night session as a crowded, theatrical assembly, following Matthew 26:65 and Mark 14:63.
art.symbolism: Tearing one's garment was a sign of grief at hearing blasphemy; here it becomes the gesture that seals the sentence. Jesus, small and still in white, is the only calm figure in the room.
art.impact: Brings out the drama and haste that Robertson saw in the night trial.

events.orderNote: Robertson treats this as an informal night session, followed by a formal vote after dawn (§157); Luke describes only the morning meeting. A night capital trial broke the later rules of the Mishnah, which Robertson takes as a sign of the council's haste, not of an unhistorical story. An ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas", found in Jerusalem in 1990, probably belonged to this high priest.

events.date: Before dawn Friday, Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: Peter denies Jesus three times
people: The maid who kept the door
events.summary: Peter follows at a distance and, through another disciple known to the high priest, gets into the courtyard, where he warms himself at a charcoal fire. A maid, then others, say he was with Jesus; his Galilean accent gives him away. Three times he denies it, the last time with an oath. The cock crows, the Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.

scripture.text: Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know the man." And immediately the cock crowed.

And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him, "Before the cock crows today, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly.

art.title: The Denial of Saint Peter
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.location: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
art.description: Three half-length figures by a fire at night. A soldier in a helmet points at Peter; the servant girl beside him points too. The aged Peter, lit from the side, turns his hands toward his own chest as he denies knowing Jesus.
art.significance: One of Caravaggio's last paintings, made in Naples in the final months of his life.
art.symbolism: Three pointing hands carry the drama: two accuse, while Peter's point back at himself. Sparks from the fire glow behind his head as the night closes in.
art.impact: Its broad, rapid brushwork shows Caravaggio's late style. The Met acquired it in 1997, and it is one of the most moving images of Peter's fall.

art.title: The Denial of Saint Peter
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: A maid holds up a candle, shielding it with her hand, to see Peter's face; he spreads one hand in denial. Two soldiers in armor look on from the left, and in the shadows at upper right Jesus can be made out among his captors, turning to look back.
art.significance: A late work, painted in the hard years after Rembrandt's bankruptcy.
art.symbolism: The candle, shielded by the maid's hand, lights Peter's face at the moment of his fall, while Christ waits in the shadows.
art.impact: One of the masterpieces of Rembrandt's late style, among the Rijksmuseum's best-known paintings.

events.orderNote: All four Gospels record three denials, but the speakers and places differ. Robertson suggests the denials ran through the hours of all three hearings (Luke notes an hour between the second and third), so each Gospel gathers them into one scene. The "other disciple" is usually taken to be John.

events.date: Friday at dawn, Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: The Sanhedrin condemns Jesus at dawn
people: The chief priests, elders and scribes
events.summary: As soon as it is day, the whole council meets again to confirm the night's verdict. Asked once more if he is the Christ, Jesus answers that from now on the Son of man will be seated at the right hand of God, and does not deny he is the Son of God. They need no further witnesses. Because only the Roman governor can order an execution, they bind Jesus and lead him away to Pilate.

scripture.text: And as soon as it was morning the chief priests, with the elders and scribes, and the whole council held a consultation; and they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him to Pilate.
And they all said, "Are you the Son of God, then?" And he said to them, "You say that I am." And they said, "What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips."

echoes.note: "Sit at my right hand, till I make your enemies your footstool."

art.title: Jesus Led from Caiaphas to Pilate
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In the early morning a jeering crowd fills a stepped street of the Upper City. Boys wave palm branches in mockery around Jesus, while a soldier leads the way and women watch from a balcony.
art.significance: Tissot imagined each step of the Passion as a separate scene, following the route he believed Jesus was taken through Jerusalem.
art.symbolism: The palm branches seem to recall the Palm Sunday welcome only days before, now turned into scorn.
art.impact: Helps the viewer picture the short, crowded walk from the high priest's house to the governor, with the whole city awake for the feast.

events.orderNote: Robertson sees this morning session as an attempt to make the night's condemnation legal. Luke says they led him "to their council", which may mean the council chamber near the Temple rather than Caiaphas' house; the exact place is unknown.

events.title: The remorse and death of Judas
events.summary: When Judas sees that Jesus is condemned, he is seized with remorse and brings the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests: "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." They will not take it back. He throws the silver down in the Temple and goes and hangs himself. The priests will not put blood money in the treasury, so they buy a potter's field to bury strangers in, and it is called the Field of Blood.

scripture.text: When Judas, his betrayer, saw that he was condemned, he repented and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned in betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
And throwing down the pieces of silver in the temple, he departed; and he went and hanged himself.
And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.

echoes.note: Thirty shekels of silver, the shepherd's wages, cast "to the potter" in the house of the Lord. Matthew credits the prophecy to Jeremiah, who also bought a field (Jeremiah 32) and went down to the potter's house (Jeremiah 18–19).

art.title: Judas Returning the Thirty Pieces of Silver
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Judas kneels, wringing his hands in despair, before the chief priests and elders. The silver coins lie scattered on the floor; the priests turn away, one raising his hand to refuse them.
art.significance: An early masterpiece painted in Leiden when Rembrandt was about 23. Constantijn Huygens praised the figure of Judas above anything from antiquity.
art.symbolism: The light falls on the priests and the great book of the Law, while Judas kneels in the half-dark: the law cannot take back the betrayal.
art.impact: It launched Rembrandt's reputation as a painter of human emotion.

art.title: Judas Returns the Money
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a colonnade of the Temple, Judas whirls round in a swirling red-brown cloak, hurling the silver coins across the pavement. Priests and elders shrink back into the shadows behind the pillars.
art.significance: One of Tissot's few scenes devoted to Judas alone, part of his Life of Christ series.
art.symbolism: The coins scattered in the air and on the floor make the "blood money" visible; Judas' wild motion contrasts with the still, watching priests who refuse it.
art.impact: Captures the despair of Matthew 27:5 more than any calm altarpiece could.

events.orderNote: Matthew places this here, though Judas may have died a little later. Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; Peter in Acts says Judas acquired the field, fell headlong and burst open. Since early times, many have read these as two sides of one event: the priests bought the field with his money, and his body fell there.

events.date: Friday, early morning, Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: Jesus before Pilate
events.summary: Early in the morning the council hands Jesus over to Pontius Pilate, but will not enter the praetorium, so as not to be defiled before the Passover. They accuse him of perverting the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar and calling himself a king. Inside, Pilate asks, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus says his kingship is not of this world and that he came to bear witness to the truth. Pilate answers, "What is truth?" and goes out to declare, "I find no crime in him."
events.journey: Less than half a mile across the Upper City, from the high priest's house to Herod's palace on the western hill (or about a mile to the Antonia Fortress, if the praetorium was there).

scripture.text: And they began to accuse him, saying, "We found this man perverting our nation, and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ a king."
Jesus answered, "My kingship is not of this world; if my kingship were of this world, my servants would fight, that I might not be handed over to the Jews; but my kingship is not from the world."

Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I have come into the world, to bear witness to the truth. Every one who is of the truth hears my voice." Pilate said to him, "What is truth?"

art.title: What Is Truth? (Christ and Pilate)
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Pilate, a heavy Roman in a white toga, stands in bright sunlight and gestures as he speaks. Jesus, gaunt and dishevelled, stands silent in the shadow, looking at him.
art.significance: Ge's realistic picture was removed from exhibition in Russia as offensive soon after it was shown.
art.symbolism: Light and shadow divide worldly power from the silent Truth standing before it.
art.impact: A key work of Russian religious realism, still debated for its stark image of Christ.

art.title: Jesus Before Pilate, First Interview
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Inside a richly furnished hall with latticed windows, Pilate in a white toga with red borders leans forward from a cushioned bench to question Jesus, who stands before him barefoot with his hands bound behind his back.
art.significance: Tissot follows John 18:33–38, where Pilate questions Jesus privately inside the praetorium while the accusers wait outside.
art.symbolism: The empty space of floor between the two men makes the conversation about kingship and truth the whole subject of the picture.
art.impact: A rare depiction of the private dialogue, which most artists pass over for the public trial scenes.

events.orderNote: Robertson divides the Roman trial into three stages: before Pilate, before Herod Antipas, and before Pilate again. John gives the private dialogue inside the praetorium that the other Gospels compress into one question. Where the praetorium stood (Herod's palace or the Antonia) is still debated; see the place note.

events.date: Friday, early morning, Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: Jesus before Herod Antipas
events.summary: Hearing that Jesus is a Galilean, Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, who is in Jerusalem for the feast. Herod, who had beheaded John the Baptist, is glad: he has long wanted to see Jesus and hopes to see a sign. Jesus gives him no answer at all. Herod and his soldiers mock him, dress him in gorgeous apparel and send him back. That day Herod and Pilate, once enemies, become friends.
events.journey: A few hundred yards within the Upper City, to the old Hasmonean palace.

scripture.text: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length; but he made no answer.
And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.

echoes.note: "The kings of the earth set themselves... against the Lord and his anointed." The early Church applied it to Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25–27).
"Like a sheep that before its shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth."

art.title: Jesus Before Herod
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Herod, in a richly patterned robe and crown, looks down from a balcony with his courtiers. In the courtyard below, a crowd throws a white cloak over Jesus and jostles him, while Roman soldiers look on and a boy picks up something to throw.
art.significance: Tissot gives a whole picture to a scene told only by Luke, setting it in a palace courtyard he imagined from his studies of Jerusalem.
art.symbolism: The white garment is Tissot's reading of the "gorgeous apparel" of Luke 23:11, a mock royal robe; Herod stays above, remote and idle, as Jesus stays silent below.
art.impact: One of the few well-known images of this brief hearing, which most painters leave out of the Passion.

events.orderNote: Only Luke records this hearing. Luke had sources close to Herod's court: Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza (Luke 8:3), and Manaen, a member of Herod's court (Acts 13:1).

events.date: Friday, about 6 a.m., Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: Barabbas, and Pilate washes his hands
events.summary: Pilate tells the priests that neither he nor Herod has found Jesus guilty. He offers, by the feast's custom, to release a prisoner: Jesus or Barabbas, a rebel who had committed murder in an uprising. His wife sends word: "Have nothing to do with that righteous man." Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd asks for Barabbas and cries, "Crucify him!" Three times Pilate protests Jesus' innocence; then, fearing a riot, he washes his hands before the crowd, releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified.
events.journey: A few hundred yards back to the praetorium.

scripture.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you, Barabbas or Jesus who is called Christ?"
Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much over him today in a dream."

So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this righteous man's blood; see to it yourselves."

echoes.note: The elders wash their hands to declare themselves innocent of a man's blood.

art.title: Christ before Pilate
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: In Pilate's crowded hall, Jesus in white stands calm while priests accuse him and the crowd shouts. Pilate, in white on his raised seat, ponders, and a man in the crowd raises his arms crying for crucifixion.
art.significance: The first of Munkácsy's huge Christ trilogy; it toured Europe and America in the 1880s and drew enormous crowds.
art.symbolism: Jesus' still, upright figure stands out against the agitated crowd; Pilate sits caught between them.
art.impact: One of the most famous religious paintings of the 19th century.

art.title: Pilate Washes His Hands
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Seen from behind, Pilate in a white toga stands on a raised platform, holding out his hands as servants pour water from a vessel. Roman soldiers and standard-bearers stand by, and beyond the arch a vast crowd fills the square and the rooftops.
art.significance: Tissot places the viewer among Pilate's guard, looking out with him at the crowd he is trying to satisfy.
art.symbolism: We never see Pilate's face: the gesture of washing, meant to declare his innocence, becomes the only thing he offers. The Roman standards show the power he could have used.
art.impact: Shows the public, theatrical side of Matthew 27:24, and the size of the feast-day crowd in the city.

events.orderNote: No source outside the Gospels mentions the Passover release. Some manuscripts of Matthew 27:16–17 call him "Jesus Barabbas"; Barabbas means "son of the father". Robertson stresses that Pilate cannot escape responsibility for his cowardly surrender, and that the guilt belongs to the plotters, not to a whole people. The Catholic Church teaches the same (Nostra Aetate 4).

events.date: Friday, about 6 a.m., Passion Week, AD 33
events.title: The scourging and "Behold the man"
events.summary: Pilate has Jesus scourged, a brutal Roman flogging with weighted whips. The soldiers crown him with thorns and dress him in purple. Pilate brings him out and says, "Here is the man!", perhaps hoping the sight will be enough, but the priests cry, "Crucify him!" When they say he made himself the Son of God, Pilate is more afraid. Jesus tells him he has no power except what is given from above. At last, seated on the judgment seat at the Pavement (Gabbatha), Pilate hands him over to be crucified.

scripture.text: Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.
So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Here is the man!"
Jesus answered him, "You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above; therefore he who delivered me to you has the greater sin."

echoes.note: "He was wounded for our transgressions... and with his stripes we are healed."

art.title: Ecce Homo
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.location: Galleria d'arte moderna, Palazzo Pitti, Florence
art.description: On a colonnaded balcony, Pilate, seen from behind in a pale toga, gestures toward Jesus, who stands with his back bare, hands bound and crowned with thorns, a red robe slipping from his shoulders. Below, a great crowd fills the square; at right Pilate's wife turns away, troubled.
art.significance: Ciseri, a Swiss-Italian academic painter, worked on this picture for many years; it is his best-known work.
art.symbolism: By turning Pilate and Jesus away from us, Ciseri puts the viewer among the officials on the balcony, facing the crowd that must answer, "Here is the man!"
art.impact: Widely reproduced in Bibles and catechisms, it shaped how many people picture John 19:5.

art.title: Behold the Man (Ecce Homo)
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: High on a balcony of the governor's palace, hung with a Roman banner, Pilate in white leans out and gestures toward Jesus, who stands beside him in a red robe and crown of thorns. A dense crowd fills the street far below, arms raised.
art.significance: Tissot, who studied Jerusalem in the 1880s, sets the scene on a tall palace facing a narrow city street.
art.symbolism: The steep height between balcony and street sets the lonely figure of Christ against the shouting mass below.
art.impact: Conveys the scale of the crowd and the public nature of John 19:5.

events.orderNote: John places the scourging and crowning before the sentence; Matthew and Mark mention the scourging with the sentence and the crowning after it (§162). John's "about the sixth hour" (19:14) seems to clash with Mark's "third hour" for the crucifixion; Robertson follows the view that John counts from midnight, Roman style, so the sentence fell about 6 a.m. The words "Ecce homo" are the Latin Vulgate of John 19:5.

events.title: The soldiers mock Jesus
people: The soldiers of the governor's battalion
events.summary: The governor's soldiers take Jesus inside the palace and call together the whole battalion. They strip him, put a scarlet or purple cloak on him, press a crown of plaited thorns on his head and put a reed in his hand. Kneeling, they salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" Then they spit on him and strike his head with the reed.

scripture.text: and plaiting a crown of thorns they put it on his head, and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!"
And they struck his head with a reed, and spat upon him, and they knelt down in homage to him.

echoes.note: "He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."

art.title: The Crowning with Thorns
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Soldiers drive the crown of thorns onto Christ's head with long staves, crowding round him on the steps before a stone arch. A bust of the emperor Tiberius looks down from above.
art.significance: Painted for the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan; Napoleon's armies carried it to Paris.
art.symbolism: The crossing rods form a cage of violence around Christ; the bust of Caesar names the power in whose name he is mocked as a king.
art.impact: A landmark of Titian's dramatic middle period, showing the influence of Michelangelo and ancient sculpture.

art.title: The Crowning of Thorns
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: In a stone courtyard, Jesus sits on a block in a red cloak, his hands chained, crowned with thorns and holding a reed. Soldiers and servants crowd round, kneeling in mock homage, jeering, and pressing the crown down with sticks; one holds a basket of thorny branches.
art.significance: Tissot follows Matthew 27:27–30 and Mark 15:16–19 detail by detail: the cloak, the crown, the reed and the kneeling mockery.
art.symbolism: The mock court around a seated "king" turns every royal sign upside down; for Christian readers the mockery speaks the truth.
art.impact: A vivid, crowded picture of the cruelty of the soldiers' game.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes that the Sanhedrin's men had mocked Jesus too (§155); Herod's soldiers did the same (§160). Pilate's soldiers were probably auxiliaries recruited from non-Jewish towns of the region, such as Sebaste and Caesarea.

events.title: The Way of the Cross
events.summary: Jesus goes out bearing his own cross. The soldiers compel a passer-by, Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, to carry it behind him; Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, as if his readers knew them. A great crowd follows, with women wailing, and Jesus tells them, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me." Two criminals are led out with him. At Golgotha they offer him wine mixed with myrrh, but he will not drink it.
events.journey: A short walk, perhaps a quarter of a mile, from Herod's palace out through a gate in the city wall to Golgotha. The traditional Via Dolorosa, walked since the Middle Ages, runs about half a mile from the Antonia.

scripture.text: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
But Jesus turning to them said, "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
So they took Jesus, and he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called the place of a skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha.

echoes.note: Isaac carries the wood for the sacrifice up the mountain.

art.title: The Road to Calvary
art.medium: Fresco
art.description: Jesus carries his cross out through the city gate, led by soldiers. Behind, at the gate, his mother tries to follow and is pushed back.
art.significance: One of the Passion scenes in Giotto's Scrovegni cycle.
art.symbolism: The procession moves to the right, out of the city, toward the Crucifixion painted next on the wall; Mary held back at the gate is the sorrow of the mother that devotion remembers in the Stations of the Cross.
art.impact: Giotto's spare, solemn storytelling influenced Passion imagery for centuries.

art.title: Simon the Cyrenian Compelled to Carry the Cross with Jesus
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Jesus, crowned with thorns, has fallen face down on the paving stones under the cross. Soldiers heave the beams off him, and in the press of the crowd a passer-by is being seized to carry it. Women kneel in grief at the right; behind, a placard with the charge is carried above the crowd.
art.significance: Tissot combines the Gospel detail of Simon with the traditional fall of Jesus on the road, one of the Stations of the Cross.
art.symbolism: Jesus lies flat beneath the full cross, a picture of the weight laid on him; the grieving women recall the daughters of Jerusalem.
art.impact: Shows the narrow city street, crowds and soldiers that make Simon's sudden conscription easy to imagine.

events.orderNote: The fourteen Stations of the Cross follow the traditional Via Dolorosa. Several stations come from tradition, not the Gospels: Jesus' three falls, his meeting with his mother, and Veronica wiping his face (a story first found in medieval writings). Robertson himself, writing in 1922, favored Gordon's Calvary as the site; most scholars today hold to the Holy Sepulchre.

events.title: The Crucifixion
events.summary: At the third hour they crucify Jesus between two robbers. He prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Pilate's title over the cross, in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, reads "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews", and he refuses to change it. The soldiers divide his garments and cast lots for his seamless tunic. Passers-by, the chief priests and the soldiers mock him: "He saved others; he cannot save himself."

scripture.text: And when they came to the place which is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on the right and one on the left. And Jesus said, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
Pilate also wrote a title and put it on the cross; it read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews."
And it was the third hour, when they crucified him.

echoes.note: "They have pierced my hands and feet... they divide my garments among them, and for my raiment they cast lots."
He "was numbered with the transgressors... and made intercession for the transgressors."

art.title: The Raising of the Cross (oil sketch)
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Three panels in Rubens' rapid sketch. In the center, straining, muscular men heave the cross with Christ nailed to it up from the ground on a steep diagonal; at left John, Mary and the weeping women look on; at right Roman officers on horseback oversee the execution.
art.significance: Rubens' preparatory sketch for his great triptych painted for the church of St Walburga in Antwerp (now in Antwerp Cathedral), soon after he returned from Italy.
art.symbolism: The diagonal of the cross cuts across the picture as the whole of human effort is spent lifting it; the three panels join grief, labor and power around the one dying man.
art.impact: The triptych made Rubens' name in Flanders and announced the full Baroque style in northern Europe.

art.title: What Our Lord Saw from the Cross
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: The scene is painted from the viewpoint of Jesus on the cross, looking down. Below are his mother, John and the other women, with Mary Magdalene prostrate at the foot of the cross. Around them stand soldiers, mounted priests and elders, and crowds on the hillside, with a rock-cut tomb in the garden behind.
art.significance: Tissot's most original composition, and the best-known work of his Life of Christ.
art.symbolism: We never see Jesus; instead we stand in his place and look at the faces of those who love him and those who mock him. The open tomb in the background quietly anticipates the burial and the Resurrection.
art.impact: Widely reproduced; its bold point of view seems to anticipate the camera angles of film.

events.orderNote: Robertson dates the crucifixion to April AD 30 (or 29). This map follows the date many scholars now prefer, Friday, 3 April AD 33; both years have a Passover that fits a Friday crucifixion. The Synoptics present the Last Supper as the Passover meal, while John places the crucifixion on the day of Preparation, when the lambs were slain; Robertson, like many harmonists, takes the Supper as the Passover meal. He follows Mark's order for the sayings on the cross: "Father, forgive them," the promise to the robber, and the words to Mary and John.

events.title: The good thief
events.summary: At first both robbers revile Jesus. Then one of them rebukes the other: they are suffering justly, "but this man has done nothing wrong." He asks Jesus to remember him when he comes in his kingly power. Jesus promises him Paradise that very day. Tradition calls him the good thief and names him Dismas.

scripture.text: But the other rebuked him, saying, "Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? And we indeed justly; for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong."
And he said, "Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingly power." And he said to him, "Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise."

art.title: The Pardon of the Good Thief
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Under a darkening sky, Jesus hangs on the cross at right; close beside him, the penitent thief turns his head toward him. The other robber hangs farther off at left above a shouting crowd, while soldiers, women and workmen with ladders fill the hill below.
art.significance: Tissot sets the thief's cross close to Jesus, so the whispered exchange of Luke 23:42–43 can be imagined in the middle of the noise.
art.symbolism: The two robbers are placed apart: one near Christ and turned toward him, one far off among the mockers, the two responses to the cross.
art.impact: A vivid picture of a scene loved in Christian devotion as the promise of mercy even at the last hour.

art.title: Christ and the Good Thief
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Christ hangs on the cross at right, his haloed head bowed toward the penitent thief, who looks up and raises his hand toward him from his own cross under a darkening sky.
art.significance: A late work by Titian, unusual for showing only Christ and the good thief.
art.symbolism: The two crosses lean toward each other: a picture of the conversation of Luke 23:42–43 and of mercy offered at the last hour.
art.impact: Shows Titian's free, loose late brushwork and his deep religious feeling in old age.

events.orderNote: Matthew and Mark say the robbers reviled him; only Luke tells of one repenting. Many harmonists take it that both mocked at first and one later changed his heart. The name Dismas comes from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, not from Scripture.

events.title: Mary and the beloved disciple at the cross
events.summary: Near the cross stand Jesus' mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. Seeing his mother and the disciple whom he loved, Jesus entrusts them to each other: "Woman, behold, your son!" and "Behold, your mother!" From that hour the disciple takes her into his own home. The Church has long seen in this gift Mary given as mother to all disciples.

scripture.text: But standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.

When Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing near, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!" Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.

art.title: The Crucifixion, with the Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist Mourning
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Two panels against a bare stone wall hung with red cloth. On the left the fainting Mary is held up by John; on the right Christ hangs on the cross.
art.significance: Painted late in Rogier's career, perhaps for a Carthusian monastery; it was probably once the wings or panels of a larger work.
art.symbolism: The bare wall and dark sky leave nothing but the grief of Mary and John and the body of Christ; mother and disciple are joined to each other as Jesus commanded.
art.impact: Regarded as one of the most moving and austere works of early Netherlandish painting.

art.title: Woman, Behold Your Son (Stabat Mater)
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: At the foot of the cross, John in white looks up at Jesus, while Mary, in blue-grey, stands with clasped hands. Mary Magdalene, in a many-colored robe, kneels and clings to the wood of the cross. Soldiers and elders stand behind.
art.significance: Tissot's French title, Stabat Mater, recalls the medieval hymn of Mary standing at the cross.
art.symbolism: The tall upright of the cross divides and joins the figures: Jesus is cut off at the top of the frame, and the scene is about those he entrusts to each other below.
art.impact: A tender devotional image of John 19:25–27, in which the Church sees Mary given as mother to the beloved disciple.

events.orderNote: Only John records this. The disciple is traditionally John, son of Zebedee. Whether "his mother's sister" is the same person as "Mary the wife of Clopas" (three women) or a fourth woman, perhaps Salome, is debated. The medieval hymn Stabat Mater meditates on this scene.

events.title: The darkness and the death of Jesus
events.summary: From the sixth hour to the ninth, darkness covers the whole land. At the ninth hour Jesus cries out the opening of Psalm 22, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", and some think he is calling Elijah. He says "I thirst", and they lift a sponge of vinegar to his mouth on a reed. Then he says "It is finished" and, crying with a loud voice, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" He bows his head and gives up his spirit.

scripture.text: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Elo-i, Elo-i, lama sabach-thani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, "It is finished"; and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
Then Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!" And having said this he breathed his last.

echoes.note: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" The psalm moves from desolation to praise.
"Into your hand I commit my spirit," a Jewish evening prayer.

art.title: The Crucifixion (Isenheim Altarpiece)
art.medium: Oil on panel
art.description: Against a black sky, the dead Christ hangs from a bending cross, his body torn and covered with sores, his hands clawed in agony. At left John supports the fainting Mary and Mary Magdalene kneels in prayer; at right John the Baptist points to Christ, with a lamb at his feet.
art.significance: The central panel of the altarpiece painted for the Antonite monastery at Isenheim, whose monks cared for victims of ergotism ("Saint Anthony's fire") and other skin diseases.
art.symbolism: Christ's ravaged body showed the sick that he shared their suffering. John the Baptist's words, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30), are written beside him; the lamb with its cross recalls "Behold, the Lamb of God."
art.impact: Often called the most powerful image of the Crucifixion ever painted, it has moved artists and writers from the 19th century onward.

art.title: It Is Finished (Consummatum Est)
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Christ hangs dead on the cross under a dark sky. Above him shines a triangle bearing the Hebrew name of God, and figures of the Old Testament, holding up scrolls, gather in the heavens around the cross. At its foot the women grieve.
art.significance: One of the few visionary images in Tissot's otherwise realistic Life of Christ.
art.symbolism: The prophets and patriarchs holding their scrolls show the Scriptures fulfilled in his death (John 19:28–30); the triangle with the divine name speaks of the Trinity and of God present at the cross.
art.impact: A rare attempt to paint the meaning, not only the appearance, of Jesus' last word in John's Gospel.

events.orderNote: Robertson orders the last four sayings: the cry of desolation (Mark, Matthew), "I thirst" (John), "It is finished" (John), and "Father, into your hands" (Luke). The darkness cannot have been a solar eclipse, which is impossible at Passover's full moon.

events.title: The veil torn and the centurion's confession
people: Mary the mother of James and Joses
events.summary: At the moment of his death the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. Matthew adds an earthquake, split rocks and opened tombs, and saints raised who appear in the holy city after his resurrection. The centurion who stood facing him says, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" The crowds go home beating their breasts, while the women who had followed him from Galilee watch from a distance.

scripture.text: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom; and the earth shook, and the rocks were split;
And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that he thus breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance and saw these things.

echoes.note: The veil that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy, which only the high priest entered once a year.

art.title: The Confession of the Centurion
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: On the hilltop outside the walls of Jerusalem, the centurion in his red cloak sinks to his hands and knees, head bowed. Around him other soldiers kneel and bow to the ground; one shades his eyes and stares upward.
art.significance: Tissot gives a whole picture to the moment the Roman officer in charge of the execution confesses Jesus (Mark 15:39).
art.symbolism: The executioners themselves end up on their knees: the first Gentile confession of faith at the cross. The city wall behind them marks the place "outside the gate".
art.impact: Brings out the reversal that Mark makes the climax of his Gospel, which begins and ends with Jesus as "the Son of God".

art.title: The Earthquake
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Under a dark sky, with the city walls and hills behind, the onlookers at Golgotha throw themselves face down on the cracked rock around the three crosses. Only the feet of the crucified are seen at the top of the picture.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 27:51–54: the earth shaking and the rocks split at Jesus' death.
art.symbolism: By cutting off the crosses at the top, Tissot makes us look down with the terrified crowd; the split rock beneath them shows creation itself responding to the death of its Lord.
art.impact: A dramatic image of a detail only Matthew records.

events.orderNote: Luke mentions the torn curtain just before Jesus' death, the others just after. In Luke the centurion says "Certainly this man was innocent!" Only Matthew tells of the raised saints.

events.title: His side is pierced
events.summary: So that the bodies will not stay on the crosses over the great Sabbath, the Jewish leaders ask Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers break the legs of the two robbers, but find Jesus already dead. One of them pierces his side with a spear, and at once blood and water flow out. John insists that an eyewitness saw it, so that we may believe. Tradition names the soldier Longinus.

scripture.text: but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
For these things took place that the scripture might be fulfilled, "Not a bone of him shall be broken." And again another scripture says, "They shall look on him whom they have pierced."

echoes.note: No bone of the Passover lamb may be broken.
"When they look on him whom they have pierced, they shall mourn for him."

art.title: The Thieves' Legs Are Broken
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Soldiers, one on a ladder and one on the ground, swing heavy clubs at the legs of the two robbers bound to their crosses. Jesus hangs dead on the cross at left, his head bowed, while women watch from below.
art.significance: Tissot follows John 19:31–33 closely, including the detail that the robbers were tied to their crosses.
art.symbolism: The violence done to the robbers sets off the stillness of Jesus, already dead, whose bones are not broken, as John says the Scripture foretold.
art.impact: Shows how the bodies were hurried down before the Sabbath, and why John stresses that Jesus' legs were spared.

events.orderNote: Robertson includes this in §167 as the proof of Jesus' death before burial. The Fathers saw in the blood and water the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist flowing from Christ's side, and the Church born from it. The name Longinus comes from later tradition.

events.title: The burial of Jesus
events.summary: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who had not agreed to its decision, takes courage and asks Pilate for the body. Pilate, surprised Jesus is already dead, confirms it with the centurion and grants it. Nicodemus brings about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. They take the body down, wrap it in linen with the spices, and lay it in Joseph's own new rock-hewn tomb in a nearby garden, where no one had yet been laid. A great stone is rolled against the door as the Sabbath begins.
events.journey: A few dozen yards from the cross to a garden tomb close at hand (John 19:41–42).

scripture.text: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.

Nicodemus also, who had at first come to him by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds' weight. They took the body of Jesus, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
And Joseph took the body, and wrapped it in a clean linen shroud, and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn in the rock; and he rolled a great stone to the door of the tomb, and departed.

echoes.note: "They made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death."

art.title: The Entombment of Christ
art.medium: Oil on canvas
art.description: Nicodemus and John lower Christ's body toward the tomb's stone slab. Behind them the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalene and Mary of Clopas grieve, one raising her arms to heaven.
art.significance: Painted for the Vittrice chapel in the Chiesa Nuova in Rome; it was taken to Paris by Napoleon and returned to the Vatican.
art.symbolism: The corner of the stone slab juts toward the viewer, as if the body were being laid on the altar: Christ's burial and the Eucharist are joined.
art.impact: Rubens and many later painters copied it; it is often counted among the greatest altarpieces of the 17th century.

art.title: The Descent from the Cross
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Two men on ladders lower Jesus' body from the cross with long linen cloths, while others reach up to receive it. The women crowd below in grief under a stormy sky, with the walls of Jerusalem behind.
art.significance: Tissot follows John 19:38–40, with Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus taking down the body.
art.symbolism: The white linen running from the crossbeam to the body anticipates the burial shroud.
art.impact: Shows how the body may have been taken down in haste before the Sabbath.

events.orderNote: Devotion (the Stations of the Cross and the Pietà) pictures Mary receiving her son's body when it is taken down; the Gospels do not say so. Arimathea is usually identified with Ramathaim, northwest of Jerusalem.

events.title: The women watch the tomb
events.summary: Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb and see where and how the body is laid. The women who had come with him from Galilee go home and prepare spices and ointments. Then, as the Sabbath begins at sundown, they rest according to the commandment, waiting to return when it is over.
events.stay: The women rested in Jerusalem through the Sabbath, Friday evening to Saturday evening.

scripture.text: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.

The women who had come with him from Galilee followed, and saw the tomb, and how his body was laid; then they returned, and prepared spices and ointments. On the sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

echoes.note: The Sabbath commandment the women keep.

art.title: The Two Marys Watch the Tomb
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Two women wrapped in mantles sit side by side on a rock ledge in an old quarry, keeping watch. The three crosses stand empty on the hill behind them against a grey sky.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 27:61: "Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the sepulchre."
art.symbolism: The empty crosses and the quiet, worn stone make a picture of waiting and grief; the women's faithful watch prepares for their visit at dawn on Sunday.
art.impact: Tissot imagined the tomb in a disused quarry near Golgotha, as archaeology has since shown the area to have been.

events.orderNote: Robertson notes that the Sabbath began at 6 p.m. on Friday, so the women's rest covered our Friday night and Saturday. Luke has them prepare spices before the Sabbath, Mark buying them after it (16:1); they may have done both.

events.title: The guard at the tomb
events.summary: The next day, the Sabbath, the chief priests and Pharisees go to Pilate. They remember that Jesus said he would rise after three days and fear that his disciples will steal the body. Pilate tells them they have a guard and should make the tomb as secure as they can. They seal the stone and set a watch.

scripture.text: "Sir, we remember how that imposter said, while he was still alive, 'After three days I will rise again.' Therefore order the sepulchre to be made secure until the third day, lest his disciples go and steal him away, and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last fraud will be worse than the first."
Pilate said to them, "You have a guard of soldiers; go, make it as secure as you can." So they went and made the sepulchre secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard.

art.title: The Watch Over the Tomb
art.medium: Opaque watercolor over graphite on gray wove paper
art.description: Soldiers keep guard at the entrance of a rock-cut tomb by lantern light. Some doze wrapped in cloaks, one sits slumped in the doorway, another lies on top of the tomb, and a sentry on the hill shades his eyes as dawn breaks.
art.significance: Illustrates Matthew 27:66, the guard set at the sealed tomb.
art.symbolism: The weary, sleeping guards and the first light on the horizon hint at what is coming: no seal or soldier will hold the tomb.
art.impact: A quiet, almost ordinary scene that makes the guard of Matthew's account easy to picture.

events.orderNote: Only Matthew records the guard, and he later tells how the guards were bribed to say the disciples stole the body (28:11–15). Pilate's words "You have a guard" can mean either the Temple police or a Roman detachment; Robertson takes it as a guard of Roman soldiers.
